steps.observation: How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual picture – from sentences to “who should look at whom?”  
Transformers replace the old idea of reading a sentence word-by-word (RNNs) with the notion that every word can, in parallel, look at every other word and decide how much it matters.  Everything else in the architecture is scaffolding that makes this “looking-at” (attention) stable, fast and trainable.

1. Token vectors – an address book  
   • Each word (or sub-word) is turned into an embedding: a fixed-length vector found in a learned lookup table.  
   • A positional code is added so the model still knows the order (because pure attention is permutation-invariant).

2. Self-attention – the core conversation  
   Pretend every token in the sentence is a person in a meeting.  
   • Query (Q): “What am I interested in?”  
   • Key (K): “What do I contain that others might want?”  
   • Value (V): “The information I’ll share if someone pays attention.”  
   For every pair of tokens i (the listener) and j (a potential speaker) we compute  
        score(i,j) = (Q_i · K_j) / √d  
   Softmax turns the scores into attention weights that sum to 1.  
   Each token’s new representation is the weighted average of the V’s it listened to.  
   Because all pairs are considered in one matrix operation, the whole layer is parallelizable.

3. Multi-head trick – looking through many lenses  
   Instead of one Q/K/V set, we make h independent sets (“heads”).  
   • Each head specialises in a different kind of relationship (synonyms, subject-verb links, long-distance dependencies, …).  
   • The resulting h vectors are concatenated and passed through a linear layer to mix them back together.

4. Feed-forward layer – local re-mixing  
   After the attention step every token goes through the same two-layer MLP (applied position-wise) to build higher-level features.

5. Residual + LayerNorm – keep the signal alive  
   Skip-connections add the input of each sub-block to its output (“x + f(x)”), and Layer Normalisation stabilises amplitudes.  Deep stacks (12, 24, 96 layers…) become trainable.

6. Encoder, decoder, encoder-decoder – variants  
   Encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa): full self-attention everywhere; used for reading/comprehension.  
   Decoder-only (GPT): the attention matrix is masked so each token can only look leftward (previous tokens); used for text generation.  
   Encoder-decoder (T5, original Transformer): an encoder builds a context, a decoder attends both to earlier outputs (masked) and to the encoder states (cross-attention); used for translation and many seq-to-seq tasks.

7. Training objective – make the meeting productive  
   • Masked-language modelling (BERT): hide a word, ask the network to guess it.  
   • Autoregressive (GPT): predict the next token.  
   • Sequence-to-sequence: predict target sentence conditioned on source sentence.  
   Gradient descent adjusts the embeddings and the Q/K/V/MLP weights so that attention patterns that help the task are amplified.

Why it works  
   • Any two positions can interact in one hop (path length 1), so long-range dependencies are easy.  
   • Parallel computation on GPUs/TPUs: all tokens processed together.  
   • Attention weights are data-dependent; the model can dynamically decide what matters for each instance.  
   • Multi-head diversity lets the model capture many relations simultaneously.

Costs and remedies  
   • Memory/time grow quadratically with sequence length (n²).  Researchers explore sparse, local, or linearised attention, chunking, etc.  
   • Positional information must be added explicitly; popular choices are sinusoidal, learned, rotary, relative.

You can think of a transformer layer as “ask everyone else what you need, aggregate the answers, then do a little private thinking.”  Stack many such layers, and you get a model that can translate, summarise, write code, or answer questions—all by repeatedly re-weighing who should pay attention to whom.
